claim: Defense against infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by CD4 T cells.
source: Defense against infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Mtb immunity.

claim: CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes have been implicated in Mtb-specific CD4 T cell responses.
source: CCR2 + inflammatory monocytes (IMs) have been implicated in Mtb-specific CD4 T cell responses but their in vivo contribution remains unresolved.
evidence: This refers to prior research findings in the field.

claim: Transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes.
source: Herein, we show that transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes, reducing CD4 T cell responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Transient ablation of IMs during infection reduces CD4 T cell responses.
source: Herein, we show that transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes, reducing CD4 T cell responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients restores Mtb transport to mLNs.
source: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients, while restoring Mtb transport to mLNs, does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
source: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients, while restoring Mtb transport to mLNs, does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs corrects CD4 T cell priming in monocyte-depleted, MHC class II-expressing mice.
source: On the other hand, transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs corrects CD4 T cell priming in monocyte-depleted, MHC class II-expressing mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes.
source: Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes but markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using zDC-DTR mice shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Specific depletion of classical DCs markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming.
source: Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes but markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using zDC-DTR mice shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes.
source: Thus, although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing expression of DC markers on transferred IMs in Figure 3B.

claim: cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
source: Thus, although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experimental approaches including adoptive transfer and depletion studies.

claim: Inflammatory monocytes express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2.
source: Inflammatory monocytes (IMs) express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2, a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IM phenotype, supported by citation.

claim: CCR2 is a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow.
source: Inflammatory monocytes (IMs) express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2, a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection.
source: Although IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection, recent studies also implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections.
source: Although IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection, recent studies also implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Experiments using CCR2-deficient mice suggested that monocytes contribute to T-cell-mediated defense against Mtb.
source: Experiments using CCR2-deficient mice also suggested that monocytes contribute to T-cell-mediated defense against Mtb.
evidence: This refers to prior experimental findings.

claim: IMs can serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection.
source: IMs, however, can also serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection, suggesting that IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection (Antonelli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection.
source: IMs, however, can also serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection, suggesting that IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection (Antonelli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from prior research supported by citation.

claim: Recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection.
source: Because recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection, it has not been possible to specifically define the role of monocytes at different times during infection (Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002; Peters et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CCR2-DTR mice were used to transiently deplete IMs and other CCR2-expressing cells during discrete stages of Mtb infection.
source: Therefore, we used CCR2-DTR mice to transiently deplete IMs and other CCR2-expressing cells during discrete stages of Mtb infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Administration of DT to CCR2-DTR mice depletes inflammatory monocytes from the lung and mLN.
source: Administration of DT to these mice depletes inflammatory monocytes from the lung and mLN
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 post infection reduces Mtb CFU in mLNs on day 12.
source: CFU counts from the lungs (C) and mLN (D) of CCR2-DTR mice given DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 and harvested on day 12.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D where DT-treated mice have reduced CFU in mLNs compared to PBS controls.

claim: DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 reduces total cell counts in mLNs on day 12 post infection.
source: Total cell counts and CD4 T cell counts in mLNs of mice on day 12 post infection after treatment with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A where DT treatment reduces total cell counts in mLNs.

claim: DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 reduces CD4 T cell counts in mLNs on day 12 post infection.
source: Total cell counts and CD4 T cell counts in mLNs of mice on day 12 post infection after treatment with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A where DT treatment reduces CD4 T cell counts in mLNs.

claim: DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 reduces ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in mLNs on day 12.
source: CCR2-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11, mLNs (B) were harvested on day 12
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and 2D where DT treatment reduces C7 T cell numbers in mLNs.

claim: DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 reduces ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in lungs on day 21.
source: CCR2-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11, lungs (C) were harvested on day 21
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D where DT treatment reduces C7 T cell numbers in lungs.

claim: DT treatment on days 7, 9 and 11 increases pulmonary bacterial burden on day 21 post infection.
source: CFU plots of lungs of mice that received naive EAST-6-specific C7 T cells and were treated with DT or PBS, as indicated, and were harvested on day 21 post infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E where DT-treated mice have higher lung CFU counts.

claim: Subsets of NK cells, dendritic cells and CD4 T cells can express CCR2.
source: Although IMs represent the most prevalent CCR2-expressing cell population, subsets of NK cells, dendritic cells and CD4 T cells can also express CCR2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCR2 expression patterns.

claim: IMs were purified from CCR2-GFP mice by sorting GFP+ cells that did not express NK1.1, CD4, FLT3 and C-kit.
source: To exclude the possibility that depletion of a non-monocyte cell population resulted in loss of Mtb transport from lungs to mLNs, we purified IMs from CCR2-GFP mice by sorting GFP+ cells that did not express NK1.1, CD4, FLT3 and C-kit.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: The IM purification strategy eliminated NK cells, CD4 T cells, dendritic cell progenitors and hematopoietic stem cells.
source: This strategy did not require antibody staining for trafficking molecules (CCR2 and CD11b) and eliminated NK cells, CD4 T cells, dendritic cell progenitors and hematopoietic stem cells, yielding a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs
evidence: This is supported by the sorting strategy and purity data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IM purification strategy yielded a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs.
source: This strategy did not require antibody staining for trafficking molecules (CCR2 and CD11b) and eliminated NK cells, CD4 T cells, dendritic cell progenitors and hematopoietic stem cells, yielding a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adoptively transferred IMs engraft in lungs and mLNs of CCR2-DTR mice.
source: CCR2-DTR mice were infected and treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received highly purified CD45.1+ IMs on days 8 and 10. (A) Mice were euthanized on day 12 post infection and flow cytometry was performed on lungs and mLNs to track the engraftment of adoptively transferred IMs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A where transferred IMs are detected in lungs and mLNs.

claim: Adoptively transferred IMs in the lung and mLN express CD11b, MHC II, CD11c and CD103.
source: The expression of cell surface markers CD11b, MHC II, CDIIc and CD103 by adoptively transferred IMs in the lung and mLN was determined.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Transfer of purified IMs to DT-treated CCR2-DTR mice restores Mtb CFU in mLNs on day 12.
source: CFU plots from day 12 mLNs of CCR2-DTR mice rescued with IMs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C where IM transfer restores CFU levels in mLNs.

claim: Transfer of purified IMs to DT-treated CCR2-DTR mice increases ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in lungs on day 15.
source: CCR2-DTR mice received a dose of naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT on days 7, 9 and 11 and received purified IMs or PBS on days 8 and 10. Lungs were harvested on day 15 and ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells were visualized.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and 3E where IM transfer increases C7 T cell numbers.

claim: CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between lungs and mLNs during Mtb infection.
source: Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs, indicating that CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between these sites (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing equivalent Mtb delivery by WT and CCR2 KO IMs.

claim: Wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs are equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs.
source: Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F by CFU analysis.

claim: C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes.
source: In contrast to our previous experiments with MHC class II-expressing recipients, C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A where MHC II KO mice receiving MHC II+ IMs do not show C7 T cell expansion.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients restores Mtb CFU in mLNs.
source: Mtb CFUs from mLNs of mice harvested on day 12.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B where MHC II KO mice receiving IMs have restored CFU levels.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II WT or MHC class II KO IMs to DT-treated CCR2-DTR mice results in similar ESAT-6-specific C7 T cell expansion in lungs on day 15.
source: CCR2-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received either MHCII WT or MHCII KO IMs on days 8 and 10. Flow cytometry was performed on lungs harvested on day 15.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C where both MHC II WT and KO IMs restore C7 T cell responses.

claim: Depletion of classical DCs on days 7, 9 and 11 reduces ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in mLNs on day 12.
source: zDC-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and cDCs were depleted on day 7, 9 and 11, and the number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells was determined in mLNs harvested on day 12.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depletion of classical DCs does not reduce CFU in mLNs of zDC-DTR mice.
source: The number of CFU in mLNs of PBS and DT treated zDC-DTR mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E where DT treatment does not reduce mLN CFU.

claim: FLT3L-deficient mice have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection.
source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F by reduced C7 T cell numbers in FLT3L KO mice.

claim: FLT3L-deficient mice lack classical DCs but not IMs.
source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs
evidence: This is established knowledge about the FLT3L KO phenotype.

claim: FLT3L-deficient mice have Mtb present in the mLN despite reduced CD4 T cell responses.
source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 by CFU analysis.

claim: Classical DCs are dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs.
source: These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is inferred from the zDC-DTR and FLT3L KO experiments showing normal CFU in mLNs despite DC depletion.

claim: Classical DCs are essential for CD4 T cell priming during Mtb infection.
source: These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is supported by data from zDC-DTR and FLT3L KO experiments showing reduced T cell responses.

claim: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs.
source: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by depletion and transfer experiments.

claim: Delivery of live Mtb to draining mLNs is an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
source: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that preventing Mtb delivery to mLNs reduces T cell priming.

claim: IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.
source: Our results extend previous reports that IMs influence CD4 T cell priming (Leon et al., 2007; Hohl et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011) by demonstrating that IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by experimental data and extends prior work.

claim: IMs differentiate into DCs in some disease models and directly prime CD4 T cells.
source: In contrast to reports from other disease models demonstrating that IMs differentiate into DCs and then directly prime CD4 T cells (Cheong et al., 2010; Zigmond et al., 2012)
evidence: This refers to findings from other studies supported by citations.

claim: IMs do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo despite acquiring characteristics of DCs.
source: our adoptive transfer studies using MHC class II KO mice reveal that IMs, despite acquiring characteristics of DCs, do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the MHC II transfer experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses.
source: Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IMs can process and present antigen.
source: Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from in vitro studies cited.

claim: Several hundred adoptively transferred IMs were recovered from the mLNs of infected mice.
source: Recovery of several hundred adoptively transferred IMs from the mLNs of infected mice also suggests that sufficient numbers of IM were present to prime T cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the transfer studies.

claim: IMs infected with Mtb may be ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to uninfected resident dendritic cells.
source: One possible explanation is that IMs, by virtue of being infected with Mtb, are ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to resident dendritic cells that have not been infected (Wolf et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings, supported by citation.

claim: Multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells.
source: A number of studies, however, have demonstrated that multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells (Itano et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD103+ DCs play a role in transport and priming during CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection.
source: Other studies characterizing CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection have demonstrated a role for CD103+ DCs in transport and priming with potential contributions by inflammatory monocytes (Bedoui et al., 2009; Edismo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs.
source: One previous study has suggested that IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs (Ersland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming during Mtb infection.
source: Our study extends this finding to live pulmonary infection with Mtb. IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Cross-dressing may play a role during Mtb infection.
source: It is possible that cross-dressing (Wakim et al., 2011), in which infected cells pass MHC molecules to uninfected cells, plays a role during Mtb infection.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism, with citation.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes was not detected.
source: We did not detect transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes.
evidence: This is a negative finding from experimental observations.

claim: The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses may be very small and below the level of detection.
source: The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses, however, may be very small and below our level of detection.
evidence: This is speculation based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection.
source: That said, given our finding that MHC class II-deficient IMs effectively complemented monocyte-depleted, MHC class II sufficient mice while MHC class II-expressing monocytes could not correct deficient T cell priming in MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted mice, we believe that transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with MHC II transfer experiments.

claim: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46.
source: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC markers.

claim: IMs do not express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46.
source: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IM phenotype.

claim: DT administration to zDC-DTR mice leads to a loss of classical DC populations.
source: To determine whether classical DCs are required for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming, we used zDC-DTR mice, in which DT administration leads to a loss of classical DC populations (Meredith et al., 2012a; Meredith et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the zDC-DTR mouse model.

claim: M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media.
source: M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media, and log phase cultures were diluted to 8 × 106 bacilli per millimeter and sonicated before infection with an aerosol exposure system (Glass-Col).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Aerosol infection was calibrated to deliver approximately 100 CFU per animal.
source: The volume of suspension, and exposure time were calibrated to deliver ∼100 CFU per animal.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice for adoptive transfer experiments.
source: Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: 2 × 10^6 purified IMs per mouse were injected via the tail vein for adoptive transfer.
source: The cells were re-suspended in PBS and 2 × 10 (Kipnis et al., 2003) cells per mouse were injected via the tail vein.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.
